lessons.scaffold-basics:
**Suspended Scaffold Basics**

Suspended scaffolds are platforms hung from an overhead structure by ropes or other non-rigid means. They allow workers to access elevated surfaces that cannot safely be reached from the ground or from supported scaffolds. Common types include two-point suspended scaffolds (swing stages) and one-point suspended scaffolds such as boatswain's chairs. They are used for exterior construction, window work, facade repair, painting, inspection, welding, and maintenance. A suspended scaffold is a complete system — every part must be selected, installed, inspected, and used correctly. OSHA requires scaffold training under 29 CFR 1926.454 to ensure workers can recognize hazards and understand control procedures.
lessons.competent-person-planning:
**Competent Person and Pre-Use Planning**

Before a suspended scaffold is assembled or used, the worksite must be evaluated. A competent scaffold person must have the knowledge and authority to identify hazards and take corrective action. The competent person assists with scaffold design, supervises assembly, verifies safe use, inspects equipment, and resolves scaffold-related safety problems. Before assembly, inspect for pipes, signs, structural projections, electrical hazards, unstable surfaces, overhead obstructions, and traffic below the work area. Workers must never guess about scaffold setup, load capacity, anchorage, tiebacks, electrical clearance, or fall protection — stop and ask the competent person when in doubt. OSHA scaffold training requirements at 29 CFR 1926.454 apply to all employees involved in erecting, operating, inspecting, and using scaffolds.
lessons.suspension-devices-anchors:
**Suspension Devices and Anchor Points**

Suspended scaffolds are supported by suspension devices attached to the structure, including cornice hooks, parapet clamps, roof irons, I-beam systems, and counterweight systems. The suspension device must match the structure and scaffold design and must be strong enough for all expected loads. The maximum intended load is the total weight of the scaffold, workers, tools, equipment, and materials that may be applied at one time. Workers must never overload a scaffold or modify suspension systems without direction from the competent person. Tiebacks must be secured to strong structural members such as I-beams or girders — never to vents, pipes, electrical conduits, or other parts that could give way. OSHA 29 CFR 1926.451 establishes general requirements for scaffold capacity, use, and suspended scaffold systems.
lessons.outrigger-tiebacks-counterweights:
**Outrigger Beams, Tiebacks, and Counterweights**

When a structure cannot directly support a suspended scaffold, outrigger beams extend from the structure to support the system. Outrigger beams must be installed at right angles to their supports unless the competent person determines another arrangement is safe. Tiebacks stabilize outrigger beams and suspension devices and must be anchored to strong structural members. Counterweights hold outrigger beams in position and must be designed for that purpose and secured against removal or dislodgment. Never use construction materials — bricks, blocks, roofing materials, buckets, or loose materials — as counterweights. Jobsite materials can be moved by other workers, shifted by vibration, or knocked loose. If a counterweight is removed, the scaffold can become unstable and collapse.
lessons.ropes-hoists:
**Suspension Ropes and Hoists**

Suspension ropes support and guide the platform during movement. Inspect ropes before and after use for cuts, kinks, fraying, broken wires, corrosion, heat damage, chemical damage, abrasion, and diameter loss. A damaged rope must be removed from service immediately. Ropes that experienced a high-speed braking incident must also be replaced even if damage is not visible. Hoists must be inspected and tested according to manufacturer's instructions before use. Gasoline-powered hoists are prohibited on suspended scaffolds due to fire and exhaust hazards. Verify that suspension ropes are long enough to reach the work level before lowering, and confirm rope ends are fitted with stopping devices to prevent the rope from running through the hoist. Scaffold platforms must not exceed their rated working load — tools, equipment, materials, and workers all count toward the load.
lessons.platforms-work-practices:
**Platforms, Boatswain's Chairs, and Safe Work Practices**

Suspended scaffold platforms must be wide and strong enough for the work being performed. Workers must not crowd the platform or overload it with materials. A boatswain's chair is a one-point suspended scaffold designed for a single worker in a seated position — it is not intended for walking or multiple workers. If welding or heat-producing work is performed, fiber rope may be unsafe and wire rope may be required. Keep the platform clean — remove trash, store tools properly, and prevent excess materials from building up. Never stand on buckets, bricks, boxes, or rails to gain extra height. Know the location of power lines and maintain required electrical clearance distances. Reposition the platform instead of leaning, stretching, or overreaching.
lessons.fall-protection-falling-objects:
**Fall Protection and Falling Object Prevention**

OSHA requires both personal fall arrest systems and guardrail systems on two-point suspended scaffolds under 29 CFR 1926.451(g). A personal fall arrest system includes an anchorage, full-body harness, lifeline, connector, and deceleration device. Vertical lifelines must be attached to an approved fixed structural anchorage independent of the scaffold — not to the scaffold platform or suspension ropes. If the scaffold fails, a lifeline attached to the scaffold could pull the worker down or transfer fall forces to other workers. Guardrails on suspended scaffolds have a top-edge height range of 36 to 45 inches. Falling object protection under 29 CFR 1926.451(h) includes toe boards, screens, and debris nets. Hard hats are the last line of defense — prevent objects from falling through engineering controls and barricading drop zones below the scaffold.

1.questionText: Which statement best describes a suspended scaffold?

options.text: A rolling scaffold frame that moves on casters or wheels
A stationary platform assembled from the ground up
A work platform that hangs from an overhead structure by ropes or other non-rigid means
A ladder system secured against a wall

2.questionText: Before beginning work on a suspended scaffold, employees are required to inspect the scaffold.

options.text: True
False

3.questionText: Which individual is responsible for identifying and correcting scaffold hazards on the construction site?

options.text: The newest member of the crew
The competent person
A third-party safety auditor
A general laborer assigned to the task

4.questionText: A tieback must never be anchored to which of the following?

options.text: An I-beam
A structural girder
An overhead structural column
A rooftop vent, pipe, or conduit

5.questionText: Using roofing materials or bricks as counterweights is acceptable provided they are heavy enough.

options.text: True
False

6.questionText: A suspension rope shows signs of fraying and corrosion. What is the correct action?

options.text: Continue using it for tasks with lighter loads
Tag it and reinspect in one week
Take it out of service immediately and notify the supervisor or competent person
Wrap electrical tape around the damaged area and continue

7.questionText: What hazard occurs if a scaffold is lowered without confirming sufficient rope length?

options.text: The descent speed increases uncontrollably
The rope can run through the hoist, removing all support from the platform
The hoist motor overheats
The platform tilts to one side

8.questionText: A boatswain's chair provides enough space for two workers to perform tasks side by side.

options.text: True
False

9.questionText: A section of the work surface is outside the safe reach of the platform. What is the correct action?

options.text: Lean over the guardrail to reach the area
Place a ladder on the scaffold platform to extend reach
Skip the area and return later in the shift
Move the platform to a position that allows safe access

10.questionText: Where must a vertical lifeline for a personal fall arrest system be anchored on a suspended scaffold?

options.text: To the scaffold platform decking
To the suspension rope near the hoist
To an approved fixed structural anchorage independent of the scaffold
To the top guardrail of the scaffold

11.questionText: Workers below a suspended scaffold are fully protected from falling objects as long as they wear hard hats.

options.text: True
False

12.questionText: Which combination of controls is most effective at preventing objects from falling from a suspended scaffold platform?

options.text: Hard hats and safety shoes for workers below
Toolbox talks and daily safety briefings
Harnesses and lanyards for all workers on the platform
Toe boards, screens, and debris nets

13.questionText: A worker's fall arrest lanyard is clipped to the scaffold guardrail post. Which response is appropriate?

options.text: Allow it temporarily since guardrails are rated for loads
Confirm the guardrail rating and allow work to continue
Stop work and redirect the worker to connect to an approved structural anchorage
Note it in the safety log for follow-up at the next inspection

14.questionText: What makes using concrete blocks or masonry materials as counterweights unsafe?

options.text: They are generally too light for suspended scaffold applications
They require special storage when not in use
They are only approved for use on smaller platforms
They can be moved or dislodged, causing the outrigger system to become unstable

15.questionText: During a pre-use check, a worker hears unusual jerking and uneven movement from the hoist. What is the appropriate next step?

options.text: Operate the scaffold slowly to see if the problem resolves on its own
Reduce the platform load by one worker and resume operations
Stop scaffold operations and report the issue for inspection before continuing
Lubricate the hoist mechanism and retry immediately
